name: Mario Villanueva
statement: Mario Villanueva is a Filipino visual artist working primarily in oil, acrylic, watercolor, and charcoal. His practice centers on quiet, observed moments—light on water, the hush of a garden at dusk, the stillness of everyday objects—rendered with a restrained palette and an eye for atmosphere. Based in Manila, he shows regularly in local galleries and artist-run spaces.

title: Quiet Tide
note: A calm stretch of shoreline at low tide, rendered in soft blues and greys. The still water reflects a pale sky, capturing the hush between waves.

title: Ember Field
note: Warm ochres and burnt oranges sweep across a small panel, suggesting dry grass caught in late afternoon light. A study in heat and stillness.

title: Low Light
note: Deep shadows and soft smudges define an interior scene at dusk. Charcoal allows the darkness to pool in corners while a single source of light holds the center.

title: Salt & Iron
note: Textured layers of salt, pigment, and metal leaf form an abstracted horizon. The surface shifts with the light, moving between cool greys and faint iridescence.

title: After Rain
note: Wet pavement mirrors the streetlamps of a quiet neighborhood. Oil on linen catches the sheen of rain and the soft glow of evening.

title: Night Garden
note: Foliage deepens into indigo and violet under moonlight. Leaves and stems blur at the edges, as if seen through a window late at night.

title: Paper Moon
note: A delicate wash of pale yellow hangs above a flat, dark landscape. Watercolor keeps the moon soft and diffuse, like light on thin paper.

title: Still Water
note: A wide, horizontal expanse of water holds a perfect mirror of the sky. The surface barely ripples, suggesting early morning before the wind rises.

title: Copper Hour
note: The brief window before sunset when light turns copper. Warm metallic tones dominate a square canvas, with shadows just beginning to lengthen.

title: Fold
note: A single gestural line folds back on itself, creating depth from minimal means. Ink on paper keeps the mark immediate and uncorrected.

title: Harbor Grey
note: Boats rest at dock under an overcast sky. Muted greys and blues describe a working harbor in quiet repose, the water still against the hulls.

title: Last Light
note: The final moments of daylight slip across a field. Gold leaf catches the last rays, set against deepening greens and shadowed earth.

title: Notes from the studio
excerpt: A look at what is on the easel this month and the ideas behind it.
body:
The easel holds a small oil study this month, something quiet and domestic—a table by the window with morning light falling across it. I have been working with a limited palette, mostly ochre, raw umber, and a touch of cadmium red, trying to let the light do the heavy lifting.

The process has been slower than usual. I scrape back more than I keep, waiting for the surface to feel settled rather than forced. What comes next is a larger canvas, likely something from the garden, but only once this small piece has told me what it needs to.

title: On color and quiet
excerpt: Why the palette stays restrained, and what a single warm note can do.
body:
I tend to keep the palette restrained—greys, blues, and earth tones for the most part. Color, when it appears, is deliberate rather than decorative. A single warm note, a patch of ochre or a thin line of red, can anchor an entire composition without overwhelming it.

This idea comes through clearly in "Ember Field," where the warmth is contained to one corner of the panel. The rest of the work stays cool and quiet, allowing that small heat to do its work without demanding attention.

title: Behind Quiet Tide
excerpt: The story of one painting, from first sketch to the final layer.
body:
"Quiet Tide" began as a small charcoal sketch made during a trip to the coast. I was interested in the flatness of low tide, the way the wet sand held the sky like a mirror, and how the horizon nearly disappeared.

The painting changed several times before it settled. Early versions had more detail—boats, a distant figure, a line of rocks—but each addition pulled the eye away from the stillness I was after. In the end I removed them, leaving only water, sand, and light, and the work finally felt finished.
